articleTitle: Ageing test of solid insulators in vacuum under the influence of electric and magnetic fields
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Ageing of dielectric materials has been studied by several researchers under different conditions. The simultaneous application of both an electric and magnetic field on the behavior of ageing of dielectric materials has not been reported so far. In this paper the effect of both electric and magnetic fields on the life of dielectric materials (paraffin solid) has been reported and a mathematical model has been presented. It is revealed from the experimental study that the lifetime of the insulating materials is increased under the simultaneous application of an electric and magnetic field.

articleTitle: Properties of water treed and non-treed XLPE cable insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Treed insulation from field aged cable is more prone to oxidation than non- treed regions, as observed by shorter oxidation induction times. This could be due to the treed region being already partly oxidized or due to contaminants within the treed regions acting as catalysts to oxidation. It is not known if the oxidation induction times vary from tree to tree, or whether eventual preferential oxidation of a treed region might lead to cable failure.

articleTitle: Effects of long-term low-level charge injection on insulating oil
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Low-level charge injection into insulating oils was maintained for six months. The permittivity of the oil was unaffected, and the conductivity-fell in response to this treatment. After the injection was stopped, the conductivity slowly rose. We conclude that, at the levels used here, charge injection will not affect dielectric constant, and will increase resistivity.

articleTitle: Partial discharge suppression in vapor-mist dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Vapor-mist dielectrics consist of very dense (∼10<sup>6</sup> droplets/cm<sup>3</sup>) mists of micron-size liquid droplets suspended in an insulating gas or vapor. They are flameproof and can have several times the uniform field ac electrical strength of SF<inf>6</inf> gas. In recent experiments these dielectrics have been found to also possess remarkable corona or partial discharge (PD) suppression properties. It was found that a brief application of vapor-mist would completely extinguish ac partial discharges at a highly stressed point electrode in atmospheric SF<inf>6</inf>. Furthermore, with the PD suppressed, the applied voltage could then be increased by more than three times without any PD activity. It is believed that the mechanisms by which the PD are suppressed include electron and ion collection by the droplets, absorption of ultraviolet radiation, and the suppression of electron emission from the electrode surface. The experimental results and PD suppression mechanisms are outlined and discussed in this paper.

articleTitle: Evolution of charge distributions in F.E.P. films analysed by the laser induced acoustic pulse method
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Very recently, new methods of determination of the spatial charge or electric field distributions in dielectrics have been proposed, opening new approaches to a better understanding of charge storage and transport phenomena in these materials.

articleTitle: A direct measurement of space charge injection in strongly inhomogeneous fields
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Dielectric ageing always starts at points of strong local field enhancement, such as sharp metallic points, inclusions and the like. In a separate contribution to these proceedings it is argued that the formation and growth of an electrical tree is governed by a balance between the electrostatic forces on the charges at points of local field enhancement and the local mechanical strength of the material. Space charge formation plays a crucial role in this ageing process. A conceivable mechanism of space charge formation is the creation of hot charge carriers by a local intrinsic breakdown mechanism, whenever the field exceeds a critical value. Eventually a thermalized cloud of trapped charges results in such a way that the limiting field is nowhere exceeded. (Field Limited Space Charge.) Space charge injection has two important consequences for dielectric ageing. First, the local fieldstrength is limited to an upper value, thus suppressing the tendency of tree formation and growth. On the other hand the hot charge carriers involved may cause local chemical degradation of the dielectric. In addition, local heating of the dielectric by periodic injection and extraction of electrons may lead to a local reduction of the mechanical strength of the dielectric, favouring the formation and propagation of electrical trees.

articleTitle: An experimental investigation of electric flashover across solid insulators in vacuum
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: In this research, we observed the characteristics of the onset of surface flashover in a vacuum for three kinds of test pieces. We also observed the development of surface flashover with good time and space resolution by using an image converter camera. The results obtained may be summarized as follows: (1) The flashover voltage varies by the condition of contact between the test piece and the electrode. In many cases, the flashover voltage sharply decreases after the first flashover. (2) The flashover voltage decreases when the dielectric constant of the test piece is increased. (3) The brightness of the flashover channel varies periodically along the channel. The periodic length is approximately 0.5 mm for our experiment. (4) The cathode spot appears when a large clearance exists between the test piece and the cathode. On the streak photographs, the bright part initiates at the cathode and moves toward mid-gap at a speed of 10<sup>7</sup> m/s, which is almost independent of pressure and applied voltage. (5) If the clearance between the test piece and the electrode is small, the cathode spot does not appear. In such a case, the flashover initiates at a point about 3 mm from the cathode, and expands toward both the cathode and the anode with a speed of approximately 1.2 × 10<sup>7</sup> m/s. (6) The calculated velocity of electron hopping on the surface is in good agreement with the expansion velocity of the bright portion.

articleTitle: Electrofracture mechanics of dielectric ageing
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: A dielectric submitted to a prolonged electrical stress will fail at nominal field levels often one or two orders of magnitude below the short term breakdown field. The damage typically consists of multiply branched hollow channels of ∼ µm diameter (electrical trees) which originate at a point of local field enhancement. Another family of damage structures consists of channels much finer in diameter and filled with water, electrolytes etc. (water trees, electrochemical trees).

articleTitle: On the Curie-V. Schweidler law in aluminumoxide
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The Curie-v. Schweidler law at low field strengths in thin films of aluminumoxide results from a volume polarization. The elementary process is caused by protons which tunnel between two metastable positions. The proton density in the samples under investigation is n<inf>pr</inf> ≈ 6.10<sup>20</sup> cm<sup>− 3</sup>.

articleTitle: Dielectric processes in heavy oils
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The electrical conductivity of Catalytic Cracking Bottoms is presented in Figure 1, as a function of temperature at 10, 100, 1000 and 10,000 Hz. It was shown earlier by Maruska et al. [2] that at elevated temperatures the conductivity is controlled by a mechanism which is independent of frequency, and thus all of the curves merge as shown. At the higher temperatures the dielectric constant also becomes independent of frequency. At lower temperatures, both the conductivity and the dielectric constant become frequency dependent. articleTitle: Spatial and temporal buildup of polarization in PVDF
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The results presented in this paper reveal a number of interesting features of the poling of PVDF: Room-temperature poling yields, depending on the applied field, no polarization at all or a spatially uniform polarization. In contrast, poling at elevated temperatures yields generally a nonuniform polarization with the poled region located close to the positive electrode at low fields, but extending almost to the negative electrode at higher fields. Another aspect of the present study is that the polarization of corona poled samples can be closely controlled by monitoring the corona currents during the poling process.

articleTitle: Influence of antioxidants on polyethylene's resistance to partial discharges in different gases
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Under the influence of partial discharges on the surface of polyethylene, a white deposit layer is always formed, irrespective of the presence of antioxidant within the investigated polymer and the type of gaseous medium in which discharges occur.

articleTitle: Hazards of insulation life estimation using censored data and high degrees of acceleration
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Insulation life studies involve considerable expenditure in terms of time and money. To keep down this expenditure, accelerated life testing is resorted to. The degree of acceleration (value of the accelerating variable) in such testing procedure should be chosen with due caution so that the life data acquired are reliable. Recently, censored data acquisition procedure has come into vogue, in which, the life test at any stress level is terminated either after a certain number of specimens fail (type 1 censoring) or after a specified length of time, subject to the condition that a reasonable number of samples fail. This procedure becomes possible in view of the extremal nature of insulation ageing. Censored testing method enables one to use lower levels of acceleration, thus reducing, considerably, the risk of faulty data entering into the analysis, but the theory and computation procedures are much more involved.

articleTitle: Mechanism of hydroxyl loss increase in gamma-irradiated and heat-treated silica fibers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The mechanism of optical loss increases in γ-irradiated and in non-irradiated fibers was investigated. It was clarified that hydrogen make bonds with germanium associated defect centers and with non-bridging oxygens, resulting in OH absorption increases.

articleTitle: 60 Hz ac characteristic of ZnO varistor below breakdown voltage
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: When an ac voltage stress is applied to a ZnO varistor in the pre-breakdown region, a through current (leak-age) constantly flows through the device. This current consists of a resistive component and a capacitive component, the magnitude of the latter being several times greater than that of the former. In spite of this relatively lower value of I<inf>R</inf>, it is the key parameter responsible for Joule heating of the device. The value of I<inf>R</inf> is greatly enhanced by external factors such as applied voltage, ambient temperature and duration time of the applied voltage.

articleTitle: Electric field - dipole interaction in poly(ethylene terephthalate)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The study of electrical properties of poly (ethylene terephthalate), (PET), has attracted great interest since it is used in commercial applications such as insulation in capacitors and as a charge storage device in foil electret transducers. For an accurate evaluation of its insulating and electret qualities the underlying physical mechanisms for charge transport have to be understood. Two processes are known to occur in PET above room temperature: (a) a dipolar relaxation at temperatures between 60° and 100°C [1,2], and (b) space charge motion [3] or increased conductivity at temperatures above 90°C [4].

articleTitle: Influence of enforced liquid motion on breakdown properties
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: It has been established by a number of investigators [1]–[4] that the statistics of breakdown of liquid dielectrics change with forced liquid motion. More specifically, the distribution of liquid breakdown voltage shifts with increasing velocity from the extreme value distribution that characterizes stationary fluids to a Gaussian distribution [2],[3]. This is quite significant from the practical point of view, since the long tail of the distribution at lower voltages is eliminated.

articleTitle: Functional analysis of antioxidant in thermoplastic cable insulations
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: DSC and CL measurements are shown to be potential tools for monitoring functional antioxidant activity in LDPE cable insulation. Data from the two procedures are consistent for unaged polyethylene samples. The results suggest that either method could be used to determine quantitatively the amount of functioning AD in the dielectric if it has no aging history.

articleTitle: Streamer initiation in liquid hydrocarbons under divergent field conditions
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: It is well established that electrical breakdown of a dielectric liquid is preceded by the initiation and propagation of streamers [1,2,3]. While considerable attention has been focused on the propagation of these streamers, little information has been published on their initiation. Rzad et al.[2] performed calculations to arrive at initiation voltages as a function of gap size for divergent field conditions. Experimental studies of streamer initiation voltages, however, have not been reported so far in the literature. This situation is probably due to the difficulties encountered in trying to observe the initiation process. This paper reports preliminary results from a detailed study of the initiation process in a highly purified liquid hydrocarbon under divergent field conditions using high spatial and temporal resolution shadowgraphic techniques. Present photographic techniques provide information on the appearance of shadows beyond the contour of the electrode without revealing the initiation site on the surface of the electrode. The photographic records published in the literature generally represent views of the whole gap yielding limited spatial resolution.

articleTitle: Field dependence of polarization in poly(vinylidene fluoride) derived from quasi-stationary poling currents
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: In recent studies,<sup>1,2</sup> switching characteristics of PVDF were investigated in the time domain by measuring charge and current responses to the stepwise application of electric fields in circuits with RC time constants smaller than 1 µS. Switching times for polarization reversal of 4 µS and larger were reported depending on the field strength and temperature.<sup>1,2</sup> Similar shapes of current vs. time curves were found in circuits with RC time constants longer than the above reported switching times and these results were also interpreted as being the characteristic switching times of the polymer dipoles.<sup>3,4</sup> More recently, we measured the poling current and the piezoelectric stress coefficient e<inf>31</inf> as functions of poling time in circuits with RC values ranging between 0.1 and 1000s.<sup>5</sup> We found that the time between the voltage application and the occurrence of polarization current maximum was proportional to the value of RC. Furthermore, the temporal buildup of the e<inf>31</inf> coefficient also scaled with the time constant. In addition to these studies, similar results were observed in hysteresis measurements at low cycling frequencies where the hysteresis loop of electrical displacement versus field strength was found to be independent of frequency.<sup>6</sup> These results suggest that it is possible to perform experiments in the quasi steady state where the time dependence of switching is not important.

articleTitle: Minimization of electromagnetic resonances in circular planar capacitive voltage dividers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Planar capacitive dividers with division ratios >10000∶1 have been developed which are suitable for measurements over the frequency range from mHz to GHz (Figure 1). The main use to date has been measurement of various phenomena in gas-insulated substations (GIS), although the devices are useful for measurements in other types of systems. Previous development has been described else-where [1] and includes selection of dielectric materials and mechanical design such that the division ratio is constant to within a few per cent from mHz to GHz. This is essential for the primary application, as the exact division ratio depends on the geometry of the position in which the divider is installed (capacitance to the conductor), and only power frequency is normally available for in situ calibration.

articleTitle: Kerr electro-optic field mapping measurements in ethylene glycol/water mixtures as a function of mixture ratio
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Because of their high dielectric constant, low cost, and ease of handling and disposal, water and water/ethylene glycol mixtures are being actively investigated for use as the dielectric in pulse power capacitors, pulse forming and transmission lines, and switches [1]. Ethylene glycol is used with water because it maintains high permittivity with a large resistivity and also allows low temperature operation without freezing [2] so that it can be efficiently used with long pulses and/or a high repetition rate. Recent charge injection analysis, terminal voltage-current measurements, and Kerr electro-optic field mapping measurements have shown significant space charge effects on the electric field distribution [3–5].

articleTitle: A nucleation mechanism for water tree formation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Any microscopic mechanism for water treeing will inevitably lead to or be based on some physico-chemical features of the microscopic nature of the trees themselves. In this model we focus on the fact that in water trees water is present neither as bulk water, which is shown calorimetrically [1], nor as a molecular dispersion [2]. Therefore we will regard [3] the formation of the water tree as being the result of a phase transformation from bulk water in a water reservoir, which is present in water filled cavities in the case of bow tie trees, or external to the insulator for vented trees. The tree-tip thus becomes the advancing phase boundary, and its growth rate is given by the phase transformation rate [3,4].

articleTitle: Relation between structure and dielectric properties of polypropylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: In the previous papers [3,4], the authors have demonstrated the existence of dependence between structural changes in polyethylene and electrical properties, caused by ageing processes. These investigations were carried out for different types of polyethylene, in the form of specially made samples as well as directly for polyethylene insulation high-voltage power cables. In order to verify that this dependence also occurs in other polymer materials, further investigations were performed on polypropylene foil. As is well known, polypropylene, on account of its good electrical, mechanical and chemical properties [1], is finding an increasing use in industry. among others in the cable industry [2].

articleTitle: Dielectric properties of polyetherimide films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The study of the dielectric properties of this polyetherimide shows that several distinct mechanisms are the source of the dielectric losses, depending on temperature and frequency. Water, which plays the dominant role at low temperatures, can be easily removed in an oven at about 100°C. Above the glass transition (∼220 °C), there is a large relaxation peak due to the motion of the main chain; this is a polar polymer. At an intermediate value, a relaxation phenomenon appears whose amplitude decreases by a factor of 2 when it is first heated. The mechanism is not fully understood but it probably involves the terminations of the molecules. The solvent has only a weak effect on these properties, provided there is less than 1 % left in the resin. Though further measurements are needed, especially on dc behavior, it is already possible to consider the polymer as a suitable material for making high-energy density capacitors for use at high temperatures. Since Tg = 220°C, a temperature such as 170°C seems to be quite acceptable for the polymer, the losses being in a reasonable range (D < 0.0025).

articleTitle: Influence of a magnetic field on the optical properties of Ba Ti O3

The results show a shift of the critical point, tending towards higher temperatures at a rate of ∼0.6 °C/KOe.

articleTitle: Materials performance study of rep rate, long life
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Materials science coupled to capacitor engineering can yield both near-term and far-term benefits. Near-term benefits include improvements in material quality and processing techniques. This can lead to improved quality control and reliability. Far-term benefits include identifying the “weak links” in the materials system (as alluded to above) and correlating these links with capacitor performance. Most important, however, will be achieving a fundamental understanding of the physics and chemistry of very high energy density, high rep rate generic processes. Only in this way will dramatic advances in capacitor technology be achieved.

articleTitle: Dielectric loss and thermoluminescence in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The principal cause of degradation in polyethylene exposed to the normal atmosphere is oxidation [1–2], thought to proceed via a free radical mechanism involving hydroperoxide intermediates. The final oxidation products are probably present mainly in the form of carbonyl groups. One of the manifestations of degradation in polyethylene is a rise in dielectric loss factor (dissipation or conductance) [2]. This can cause serious attenuation of signal strength in telecommunications coaxial cables, since they frequently contain spacers fabricated from polyethylene. Although the attenuation is fairly readily measured between repeater stations, direct dielectric loss measurements on individual spacers are hampered by their small surface area (typically 0.5cm <sup>2</sup>).

abstract: A multi-conductor transmission line model is developed to represent the line-end coil of a winding under surge conditions. Transmission line parameters are calculated and surge voltage at any point within the line-end coil is predicted for a given surge and termination. The influence of inclusion of the rotor, variation in the slot length and location of the coil side in the slot, on maximum interturn voltages within the line-end coil is examined.

articleTitle: Partial discharge characteristics in layered barium titanate structures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Pd characteristics for MLC capacitors with different relative permittivities, porosity, and void size distributions were evaluated. The results show that: 1. Pd is a strong function of and increases with the increase of the applied field. 2. Higher dielectric constant, which gives a bigger field enhancement, also enhances the Pd activity. 3. The source of Pd is the ionization discharge across the voids in the bulk as well as those adjacent to the electrodes. Knowing the void size distribution, the Pd characteristics are generally predictable. 4. The cause of low breakdown for a dielectric with high porosity is that the regions of thin dielectric associated with porosity cannot withstand a high field as the voltage across a void drops significantly by the partial discharge.

articleTitle: Study of the electrical history of partial discharges in solid dielectric
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: An experimental study on the electrical history of the charge-voltage characteristics of voids in a plexiglass dielectric material is reported. It has been found that, at the same applied voltage, the discharge magnitude obtained while the voltage is decreasing is lower than the corresponding magnitude obtained with the increasing applied voltage. This indicates that the Q-V characteristic exhibits a hysteresis phenomenon. The phenomenon is attributed to the energy stored in the cavity. A mathematical model is developed to explain the effect of the electrical history of the discharge and will be presented at the meeting.

articleTitle: Characterization of vapor-phase photopolymerized MMA
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Recently photochemical vapor depositions have attracted attentions as the formation method of thin films at low temperature with small amount of impurity and irradiation damage. In studies of photochemical vapor deposition, the thin film formation of inorganic substances, such as silicon dioxide (SiO<inf>2</inf>), silicon nitride (Si<inf>3</inf>N<inf>4</inf>), amorphous silicon and various kinds of metals have been reported<sup>(1)∼(5)</sup>. Mercury lamp and ultraviolet laser are used as the light source which causes the photochemical reactions. This method utilizes the vapor-phase reactions and is different from the conventional method depending on solid- or liquid-phase reactions. This method is being expected to apply to the manufacturing process of microelectronic devices such as semiconductors, instead of plasma chemical vapor deposition.

articleTitle: Aging in glass fiber lightguides

abstract: This paper briefly reviews three areas of concern relating to aging effects in silica-based lightguides. In all cases, further work is necessary to quantitatively predict the lifetime behavior of lightguides in a given operating environment.

articleTitle: Effect of an electric field on the infrared spectra of polymers

abstract: If a molecular dipole vibrates in such a way that the change in its dipole moment makes an angle θ with the direction of propagation of the IR radiation, then the absorption of IR by the dipole is proportional to sin<sup>2</sup>θ [6]. Over the whole sample the absorption will depend on the sample average <sin<sup>2</sup>θ>. Thus if an electric field is applied in the same direction as the IR propagation, then dipoles whose change in moment moves into alignment with the field will exhibit decreased peak height, while those which move out of alignment will show increased peak height. (In the present context a “peak” is an absorption peak which corresponds to a transmission minimum.)

articleTitle: The ferroelectric nature of a phase transition in a copolymer of vinylidene fluoride and tetrafluoroethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The ferroelectric properties of poly(vinylidene fluoride) [1] have recently stimulated interest in similar properties of its copolymers with other fluorocarbons. While copolymers with trifluoroethylene have been studied extensively from a ferroelectric viewpoint, (e.g. ref. 2–5), others have not. Yet, copolymers with tetrafluoroethylene are of particular interest in relation to the homopolymer because they do not introduce new chemical species (-CHF-) or tacticity defects as does trifluoroethylene, and because they can be viewed simply as PVF<inf>2</inf> containing an increased amount of head-to-head (-CF<inf>2</inf>-CF<inf>2</inf>-) defects. [6,7] Poling of such a vinylidene fluoride/tetrafluoroethylene copolymer (hereafter abbreviated VF<inf>2</inf>/F<inf>4</inf>E) was shown through the IR studies of Latour [8] to involve dipolar realignment which was used by Stefanou [9] to account for the observed piezoactivity. The pyroelectricity of such a copolymer was compared to that of PVF<inf>2</inf> [10], and pyroelectric, piezoelectric, and charge-transport studies showed highly inhomogenous polarization across the thickness of such copolymer films [11]. Ferroelectric studies by Hicks et al. [12] and Tasaka and Miyata [13] revealed hysteresis loops but no Curie transition, while an increase in the dielectric constant with temperature [12,14] was related to ionic impurities. However, in a recent report [15] we provided evidence for a Curie transition in a VF<inf>2</inf>/F<inf>4</inf>E copolymer quenched to 0°C. A subsequent report [16] shows evidence for the solid state transformation using dielectric and thermal techniques as well as X-ray.

articleTitle: Radiation resistance characteristics of image guides
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The effects of γ-ray radiation of <sup>60</sup>Co on two optical fibers having different OH concentration and a bundle fiber have been investigated in the visible region. The radiation induced attenuation increases with the increment of total irradiation dose exhibiting peaks at around 460 nm and 600–630 nm in the optical fibers having OH. It has been found that radiation induced loss is related linearly to the toal dose in all cases. However, the induced loss in the image bundle fiber is about 1100 dB/km for a total dose of 2×10<sup>6</sup> rads at 500 nm with the radiation rate 4×10<sup>5</sup> rad/hr, this induced loss is about 3 times higher than the optical fiber of the same material. This loss difference is expected to vanish with the suitable fabrication condition.

articleTitle: Hydrostatic pressure effect on the electrical conductivity of low density Polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Low density Polyethylene (LDPE) plays an important part in high voltage cable insulation, particularly in submarine d.c power transmission lines. In this particular case, it is worth observing the behaviour of this material under conditions similar to its real application. Conductivity measurements of LDPE as a function of hydrostatic pressure helps us understand the breakdown mechanism in this material, and check some breakdown theories based on the electromechanical, free volume, electronic or thermal breakdown processes (1) (2) (3) (4) (5).

articleTitle: Loss increase of optical fibers due to hydrogen from coating resin
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: 1. One of the major origin of H<inf>2</inf> generation in jacketed fiber is confirmed to be the decomposition of residual Si-H groups in the silicone resin of the coated fiber, by the methods of Infra-red absorption analysis, Gas chromatograph analysis and the study of increase in loss spectra.

articleTitle: Electric conduction in polyethylene between conductive fluid electrodes
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: It is well known that most fluids of low viscosity are penetrable into polyethylene and that some fluids such as acetophenone and silicone oil used as additives have the capability of inhibiting tree initiation or growth in polyethylene. Additives having such a capability are attractive to the insulation industry because the inhibition of tree initiation or growth implies the extension of the service life of polymeric-insulated apparatus and systems. It is generally believed that trees are initiated in the regions of highly localized electric fields, and that the action of additives is a stress-grading process activated either by field-enhanced dissociation [1,2] or by field-enhanced ionization [3,4]. Although such a stress-grading mechanism has long been used to elucidate the tree inhibition phenomenon, it is not unique and also not consistent with other features related to this phenomenon, indicating that a clear understanding of the behaviour of additives in polyethylene still remains to be obtained. To examine the stress-grading mechan2sm and to probe other more appropriate mechanisms, we have carried out an investigation into this problem from a different angle by studying electric conduction in polyethylene between conductive fluid electrodes in the hope that this would provide further insight into the behaviour of additives in polymers.

articleTitle: Open-circuit voltages and their influences on the dielectric properties of metal-dielectric-metal systems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: On heating metal 1-polymer- metal 2 systems above room temperature, open-circuit voltages are generated between the two dissimilar electrodes [1–4]. Ieda et al. [1, 2] were the first to suggest that these open-circuit voltages, V<inf>oc</inf>, were of electrochemical origin. Several other explanations of the phenomenon have been put forward [3–6] but most of them neglect the central fact, i.e. the oxidation of electrodes. In that respect, open-circuit voltages depending on the differences in work function of the electrode metals [4] are meaningless.

articleTitle: Dielectric characterization of magnetite-loaded toners
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: In most xerographic copy processes, the latent electrostatic image on a photoconductor is developed (toned) in the development nip by bringing the photoconductor into contact with a continuous supply of flowing developer material. The dry ink (toner) is either already charged or becomes charged by the electrostatic field of the image itself and is then attracted to the image. The dielectric behavior of the developer layer in the nip is very important, because such parameters as dielectric constant and effective relaxation time determine the development field, process time constants, etc. Characterization of single-component xerographic developers is complicated by several factors. The materials are granular, typically composed of a polymer resin with dispersed pigment, and sometimes magnetite or flow agents. A further complication is that the toner in the nip is flowing and sometimes strongly coupled by magnetic or electrical forces. The effects of flow and agitation on charge transport in xerographic developers is largely unknown.

articleTitle: Chemical changes in polyethylene by high energy ions
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Corona consists of a cloud of ions and electrons. The energies of these ions and electrons range from those approximating bond energies of the order of 2.2 to 4.3 eV for some corona in small voids to energies orders of magnitude greater than bond energies for some plasmas. When corona causes insulation erosion, the energies of some of the ions and electrons impinging on the insulating material are certainly greater than bond energies.

articleTitle: Investigation of mobile ions in polyimide films using MPOS structures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Polyimide (PI) has been widely used in integrated circuits and semiconductor devices as multilevel insulators and surface-passive materials (1.2). As the sodium ions and other alkali metal ions are the major factors of instability of semiconductor devices, the investigation of migratory characteristics of sodium ions in PI has aroused great interest among insulation researchers. Unfortunately, at higher temperatures the electronic conductivity in PI increases rapidly, so that the ionic and electronic currents cannot be effectively separated in the case of conventional metal-PI-metal(MPM) structures. In this respect, the metal-PI-SiO<inf>2</inf>-silicon(MPOS) structures have proved to work satisfactorily.

articleTitle: Spark laws for the electrical breakdown in liquid hydrocarbons
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Nano-second time resolved current and voltage measurements were carried out for the the spark breakdown of liquid n-hexane, n-decane, n-pentane, and neohexane. The test cell consisted of a coaxial tip-plane electrode assembly with integrated voltage dividers and current shunt. DC-voltage was applied at a rate of 0.29 kV/s until breakdown occurred. The current and voltage signals were fed into two analog-digital-converters and further processed by a computer. The evolution in time of the spark resistance, R<inf>s</inf>(t) showed a similar behavior in all the liquids investigated, and an analytical function for R<inf>s</inf>(t) was derived.

articleTitle: Photoemission study in modified Millikan apparatus: Application to poly(N-vinylcarbazole)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: For a long time poly(N-vinylcarbazole) has served as a model of a polymeric photoconductor and a great deal is known of its electrical properties, especially of charge carrier generation and transport [1]. The detailed electronic structure of this material, and of most amorphous polymers, is, however, not yet clearly understood.

articleTitle: Positive charging of fluorinated ethylene propylene copolymer (Teflon FEP) by irradiation with low energy electrons
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Surfaces of materials irradiated by an electron beam emit low-energy secondary electrons and backscattered primary electrons. The total emission yield. defined as the ratio of the number of emitted electrons to the number of incident electrons. increases with decreasing primary energy. At the second crossover point this ratio equals unity and with further decreasing energy the emission yield reaches a maximum and then decreases until it again becomes equal to unity at the first crossover point. The net current in the investigated material changes its polarity at the first and second crossover point (1).

articleTitle: Test techniques for model development of repetitive service energy storage capacitors
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Advanced development in repetitive pulse capacitor technology has produced new testing requirements that include high-average power modulator test platforms and developed instrumentation.

articleTitle: Hot electron transport and dielectric breakdown in polymeric dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: A new technique for directly measuring the energy and momentum loss rates of hot electrons as a function of their kinetic energy E in dielectrics is presented. The relation between the dielectric breakdown on one side, the momentum scattering rate γ<inf>p</inf>(E) and the LO phonon emission rate γ<inf>u</inf><sup>LO</sup>(E) of hot electrons on the other side is essential and direct and can be seen through the expression equation which controls the properties of hot electrons in an electrical field F. Indeed, this integral is the only non-trivial term in the equations yielding their energy distribution and their ionization rate in an insulator with an ionization energy large compared to the energy loss per scattering event [1].

articleTitle: Solitary electron compression waves launched by increasing electron injection into dielectric fluid

abstract: Periodic trapping and detrapping of electrons with field assistance in a Newtonian dielectric fluid will account for the principal phenomena of the RVA technique by a modified steady EHD flow mechanism having strong similarity to electromagnetic processes.

articleTitle: Influence of electron impact energy and dielectric permittivity on surface flashover in vacuum
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The dependence of the surface flashover of a solid dielectric insulation on the secondary electron impact energy and the dielectric permittivity is studied in vacuum. Applied voltages of dc, ac (60 Hz) and 1.2/50 µs lightning impulse have been used. The surface flashover in vacuum is calculated for different dielectric materials and compared with the experimental values. Good agreement is obtained.

articleTitle: Ac minimum flashover voltages and wave number of occurrence of local discharges prior to flashover on polluted insulators
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The relation between ac minimum FO voltages V<inf>ℓ</inf> and voltage build-up rates B has been investigated with respect to the wave number of occurrence N of local discharges prior to FO. The results show that V<inf>ℓ</inf> occurs when N equals N<inf>ℓ</inf> (5∼11); i.e. N<inf>ℓ</inf> increase from 5 to 11 as the pollution levels increase, and is independent of lengths for a given width. Additionally, similar informations are obtained for the cyclic number of ac minimum reignition voltages in contaminated conditions. It is also shown that the relation between the minimum FO voltages and the wave number of occurrence of local discharges is able to explain qualitatively with respect to the accumulation of Na atoms in discharge space at FO.

articleTitle: Analysis of gaseous decomposition products of polyethylene exposed high fields and partial internal discharges
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Although it is well known that divergent electric fields, such as produced by the needle-plane geometry, will generate tree-like breakdown channels that, in time, penetrate the dielectric, such channels are not seen under uniform field conditions. Further, it is also known that the electrical treeing process is accompanied by internal discharges which are readily detected by electrical and optical means [1,2]. It was of interest to learn if the route to breakdown under uniform and divergent field conditions involved similar decomposition processes in the dielectric. A mass spectrometer was employed to detect the gaseous species emitted by samples exposed to high AC stresses applied in a vacuum chamber attached to the spectrometer head.

articleTitle: Uniform field breakdown of fluorocarbons and other gases
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The breakdown voltage of several fluorocarbons follow the simple empirical law proposed a few years ago for simple gases. Several fluorocarbons show breakdown voltages higher than, or similar to, that of sulfur hexafluoride and constitute serious candidates as replacement gases.

articleTitle: Ac reigniting discharge characteristics on contaminated insulator surface
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The characteristics on the reignition and the arc voltages which were measured under both the contaminated and the non-contaminated (in air) conditions have been discussed. The results obtained are as follows; [1] With increase of the cycle number of reignitions, the reignition voltage v<inf>r</inf> and the arc voltage v<inf>a</inf> decrease to a minimum value and then increase again. The trend is independent of whether the insulator surface is contaminated or not. [2] The minimum value v<inf>R</inf> of reignition voltages v<inf>r</inf> occurs in larger cycle number of reignition than the minimum V<inf>A</inf> of the arc voltages v<inf>a</inf>. This means, more reignitioncycles are required for the voltage v<inf>R</inf> than for the voltage V<inf>A</inf>. [3] When the arc current i<inf>A</inf> is larger, the voltage v<inf>R</inf> occurs in smaller cycle number of reignition. [4] The voltage v<inf>R</inf> in air occurs in smaller cycle number of reignition than that under the contaminated condition. When the insulator surface is not contaminated, voltages v<inf>r</inf>, after the minimum v<inf>R</inf> is attained, cease to rise rapidly and remain constant approximately. [5] Under the partially contaminated condition, the voltage v<inf>R</inf> seems to occur in slightly smaller cycle number of reignitions than that under the whole gap contaminated condition. [6] The cycle numbers for the voltages v<inf>R</inf> and V<inf>A</inf> seem to approximate to that obtained by the other contaminating test method. [7] Under the contaminated condition, when the arc current is about 0.6 A or below, the reignition voltage v<inf>R</inf> is proportional to the −1 power of the arc current. The arc voltage V<inf>A</inf> also shows the same characteristic as the voltage v<inf>R</inf>, when the arc current is about 0.35 A or below. [8] In air, both the voltages v<inf>R</inf> and V<inf>A</inf> are expressed in proportion to the −0.7 power of the arc current, and the values become extremely higher than that under the contaminated conditions.

abstract: The eight cycloaliphatic components exposed for three years to environmental aging have shown a satisfactory be haviour, since the electrical and thermal characteristics have not suffered appreciable variations. The morphological analysis has not evidenced sensible plasticization phenomena, or in general, modifications of the chemical structure. Only a change in sample colour without loss of hydrophobicity and a light surface erosion is present, as shown by SEM micrographs of fig.5.

articleTitle: TSC due to space charge in polyvinylidene fluoride
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: Unstretched and uniaxially stretched PVOF showed TSC peaks due to space charge above room temperature. The TSC results revealed that the space charge was positive homo space charge injected from the anode. The space charge was found to play an important role in the piezoelectricity of PVOF. The high field conduction of PVOF was strongly modified by homo space charge which suppressed the hole injection.

articleTitle: Development of a temperature compensated PVDF transducer for dynamic pressure measurements
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The pressure sensing element of the transducer, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), has been the subject of many laboratory studies and has been used in many applications during the past decade [1–5]. Since the poled active material is both pyroelectric-and piezoelectric, measurements are usually carried out in an isobaric or isothermal environment so that only one effect is activated. For the measurement of dynamic pressures, an isothermal environment is not always present because pressure pulses will be accompanied by temperature pulses due to adiabatic compressional heating. This effect was discussed by DeReggi et al. who considered the relative time effects of pressure induced temperature changes in PVDF and temperature changes which occur in the surrounding medium [6]. Adiabatic heating of the PVDF will occur in coincidence with its pressure change. When adiabatic heating of the surrounding medium occurs, the thermal time constant, τ, for diffusion of heat into the transducer will determine its pyroelectric response as a function of time. If the temperature changes in PVDF and its surroundings are identical, then there will be no heat transfer and the pyroelectric response will be due to adiabatic heating of the PVDF only. Calculations for this special case show that the pyroelectric charge signal is approximately 8% of the piezoelectric charge [6]. In general, adiabatic heating in both PVDF and its surroundings along with the time scale of each effect must be considered. For pressure measurements at t ≪ τ temperature compensation can be achieved by applying the 8% correction to the transducer signals. For longer times the conduction of heat from the surroundings must be measured in order to apply the appropriate correction to the electrical signal from the PVDF gage.

articleTitle: Radiation resistance of pure silica core optical fibers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The influence of the kinds of impurities in the core and manufacturing process of the core on the radiation resistance was investigated for 6 kinds of pure silica core optical fibers. We have obtained the following results: 1. The radiation resistance of OD doped fiber was good and the initial loss before irradiation was low also although the total hydroxide molecule content was low. on doped fiber will be promising as the radiation resistant optical fiber in a future. 2. The induced loss characteristic varied very much according to the kinds of impurities and the manufacturing processes even in the pure silica core fiber: The induced loss characteristic of each kind of fiber was much different especially according to the difference in photo power. The photobleaching effect of fiber No. 4 manufactured by the MCVD method was quite low, but fiber No. 5 and 6 manufactured by the plasma method was rather high. To put it more concretely, the induced loss of No. 5 had the difference of 20db/100m and 2db/100m respectively according to the different measurement condition of 0.14 µ w and l4 µ w. Measurement conditions should be standardized for the measurement of the radiation resistance of optical fibers, especially with respect to photo power etc, because of photobleaching effect.

articleTitle: PVDF and related co_polymers, their structural and electrical properties as criteria in electrical insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: PVDF and its copolymers have been developed very recently and therefore there are only few manufacturers is the world. Because of unique structure these materials are able to sustain harsh thermal, chemical, electrical and even ultraviolet environment. Low smoke and low flame spread make their use possible in plenum as well as in computer wiring and host of equipments as mentioned earlier. This is the reason why they are receiving much attention of material scientists.

articleTitle: Induced loss characteristics in silicone clad pure silica core fiber under gamma radiation — relation between the NBOHC and the 2.0 eV band —
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: We obtained that the defect center responsible for the 2.0 eV band is the NBOHC. Two kinds of the NBOHC (NBOHC:Si and NBOHC:H) were proposed based on the experimental results.

articleTitle: Hydration effects and electrical conductivity in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1984
abstract: The presence of atmospheric moisture or humidity has long been known as a catalyst, or even an initiator, of dielectric breakdown in insulators, especially about the surface. The role played by the water molecules is largely unknown possibly because the way in which it binds to insulators such as polyethylene, in its various forms. Furthermore, the mechanisms responsible for surface conductivity remain a matter for considerable speculation [1–3] even in dry materials. The situation is likely to be far more complex in the presence of water vapour.
